cells: The Oracle Problem in Software Testing: A Survey (Barr, Harman, McMinn, Shahbaz and Yoo, IEEE TSE 41(5):507-525, May 2015) — https://philmcminn.com/publications/barr2015.pdf
the survey's own definition and taxonomy of test oracles and oracle strength; not any benchmark's grader

doi 10.1109/TSE.2014.2372785; author (coauthor McMinn) copy archived whole, 773,275 bytes, sha256 6c5689497594a75f08c1b37b3dd361e11c54946bbbf79f670d660f5d298d3d51; Introduction, sentence at pdftotext lines 27-29 of the archived extraction: "a procedure that distinguishes between the correct and incorrect behaviors of the System Under Test (SUT)" (16 words)

the oracle-strength question is defined as distinguishing correct from incorrect behavior, so an assertion that only checks a path exists is an oracle that cannot distinguish — the survey is the umbrella taxonomy (explicit, implicit, partial and pseudo oracles) under which presence-only grader tests sit
State of Mutation Testing at Google (Petrovic and Ivankovic, ICSE-SEIP 2018) — https://static.googleusercontent.com/media/research.google.com/en//pubs/archive/46584.pdf
Google's own account of mutation-based test-quality measurement at scale; not any benchmark's grader

ICSE-SEIP 2018, doi 10.1145/3183519.3183521; Google archive PDF archived whole, 419,943 bytes, sha256 c128ccd374906ade3e4e885dbfb685bc7268ee92ccf4c8d71f678b17e3cdbcca; section 1 Introduction paragraph 2, pdftotext lines 74-76 of the archived extraction: "coverage alone might be misleading, as in many cases where statements are covered but their consequences not asserted upon" (19 words)

the industrial name for the presence-only gap is coverage whose consequences are not asserted upon, and mutation analysis is the established industrial measure for it — prior art for judging a grader test by whether it can detect a change to the artefact it scores

Assessing Oracle Quality with Checked Coverage (Schuler and Zeller, ICST 2011) — https://www.st.cs.uni-saarland.de/publications/files/schuler-icst-2011.pdf (host unreachable 2026-10-28; read via Wayback snapshot 20260422011919id_)
checked coverage and the paper's own assertion-removal experiment; not any benchmark's grader

ICST 2011, doi 10.1109/ICST.2011.32; Wayback copy 1,492,763 bytes, archived as pages 1+6 slice, 751,031 bytes, sha256 8a072dd58717fc853cc9283b918b03515aaccc80376ac4793dc7c50c66b16958 (full copy exceeds the 1 MiB cap; the quoted page is inside the slice); assertion-removal paragraph at slice-pdftotext lines 239-240: "test suites with no assertions still detect a significant fraction of the mutations (43 % on average)" (17 words)

removing every assertion still leaves 43 percent mutant detection through implicit runtime checks, so a pass proves less than it looks and checked coverage names the statements an oracle actually influences — the direct instrument family for measuring how little a presence-only test checks
Mind the Gap: The Difference Between Coverage and Mutation Score Can Guide Testing Efforts (Jain and Kalburgi) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.02395
the paper's own oracle-gap definition and observational argument, not its later revisions

arXiv:2309.02395v1 (5 Sep 2023); Introduction, pdftotext lines 80-82 of the archived extraction, sha256 8719ebae726001f4551a6555f9e988003e155f58e74bb0ee67481e415b928024: "We define the oracle gap as the difference between source code coverage and mutation score for a given software element" (20 words)

the covered-but-not-asserted distance already has a published name, the oracle gap, and the same text says naive tests that cover code without strong assertions straightforwardly produce positive gap — a ready-made metric for presence-only grader tests
Beyond Coverage and Mutation: A Blind-Spot Analysis of LLM-Generated Unit Tests (BlindSpotEval, ObligBench) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32548
the framework's own obligation-based metrics and reported blind spots, not external validation

arXiv:2610.32548v1 (23 Oct 2026); Abstract sentence at rendered line 244 of the archived full-text HTML, sha256 7b1bd3d05941eedd411924ceb6f2d0e58a3ce26e89bcff5fb89e505201045232: "Oracle strength is high on average but uneven, with weaker assertions for object return property values and exceptions." (18 words)

oracle strength is measured per assertion obligation and its killed-mutant count explicitly excludes incidental crash and exception kills so accidental failures do not inflate assertion strength — the same discipline a presence-only grader classifier must apply to exit-status passes
Mutation-Guided Unit Test Generation with a Large Language Model (MUTGEN; Wang, Xu, Briand and Liu) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.02954
the paper's own reported coverage-versus-mutation-score finding, not its tool's effectiveness

arXiv:2506.02954 (v1 3 Jun 2025; IEEE TSE acceptance stated on the abs page comments); Abstract at rendered line 124 of the archived abs page, sha256 d47c8464bdf4c8d5933e30558ae4d496c0d189ee7a1e320baace9449344af1e8: "some test suites achieve 100% coverage but only 4% mutation score" (13 words)

a measured case of suites that pass while constraining almost nothing — 100 percent coverage against a 4 percent mutation score — direct precedent that a passing grader test can be presence-only in effect

Assertion Roulette at XUnitPatterns.com (Gerard Meszaros, xUnit Test Patterns companion site) — http://xunitpatterns.com/Assertion%20Roulette.html (site unreachable 2026-10-28; read via Wayback snapshot 20250118170143id_)

Wayback 2025-01-18 snapshot of the smell page, gzip-decoded, 18,201 bytes, sha256 e6264bc28447a2d343eecfdbfed7b9388b7bef390ffbf3d555d73a33ca9d32ed; smell definition sentence at line 78 (byte offset 3886): "hard to tell which of several assertions within the same test method" (12 words; the next words are tab-separated in the HTML)

Can we find bugs using LLM-generated oracles? (Konstantinou, Degiovanni and Papadakis; v1 2024-10-28 titled Do LLMs generate test oracles that capture the actual or the expected program behaviour?) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.21136

Do Androids Dream of Breaking the Game? Systematically Auditing AI Agent Benchmarks with BenchJack — https://arxiv.org/html/2605.12673v1
the paper's own adversarial audit of ten agent benchmarks — its exploit classes, per-benchmark hack rates and the Terminal-Bench result — not any TB2 task's grader bytes

arXiv 2605.12673v1, §5.1 Benchmark Hackability, archived HTML line 809: "Simple exploits can drive the hack rate to near-perfect on nine of the ten benchmarks, including Terminal-Bench, SWE-bench Pro, and SWE-bench Verified." (22 words; archive trimmed at 1 MiB, quote inside; sha256 9164745f…5dee)

synthesized reward-hacking exploits reach near-perfect scores on nine of ten audited agent benchmarks including Terminal-Bench without solving any task, and an iterative generate-patch loop cuts the hackable ratio below 10 percent — a whole-benchmark adversarial audit, not a per-test static classifier of graders
Maintaining Benchmarks Against Increasingly Capable Agents: Detection and Remediation of Unearned Passes — https://arxiv.org/html/2609.34262v1

The Verification Horizon: No Silver Bullet for Coding Agent Rewards — https://arxiv.org/html/2606.26300v1

arXiv 2606.26300v1, §2.1 Preliminary Reward Faithfulness, archived HTML line 423: "the absence of false positives (an incorrect solution passes the tests) and false negatives" (14 words; sha256 08fc5c5c…25d43)
